readerTitle: Three plans by Friday: pricing software for restaurants
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (식당용 예약 소프트웨어 스타트업). 고객은 식당, 판매자는 소프트웨어 회사라 두 업종을 한 이야기로 다룸. 모든 수치는 설명용.
insight: 요금제 세 개는 가격표가 아니라 질문 세 개에 대한 답이다. 무엇에 따라 가격이 커지는가, 누구를 위한 요금제인가, 단계별 가격 차이가 가치 차이와 맞는가.
misconception: 요금제는 기능을 조금씩 더 얹고 가격을 조금씩 올리면 된다. 단계가 많고 가격 차이가 작을수록 고객이 편하게 고른다.

sources.text: 가격 구조의 표준 개념 (가치 단위 과금, good-better-best 요금제, 고객 스스로 고르는 가격 차별, 앵커링)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 가격과 예약 한도는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 요금제 간 비율 확인: Basic $39 → Plus $99 (약 2.5배) → Group $299 (약 3배). 카드 3, 4, 5의 숫자가 서로 일치하는지 다시 확인하세요.
출시 후 결과(카드 6)는 가상 서술이며 실제 전환율이나 통계를 암시하지 않도록 수치 없이 썼습니다. 실제 데이터처럼 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Three plans by Friday
body: Mira built table-booking software for restaurants. Ten local places have used it free for six months. A small café, two busy bistros, a pizza chain with four sites.
Now the free beta ends. She needs three plans by Friday, and every choice will decide who stays, who upgrades and who leaves. You're making the calls.

image.label: A founder at a restaurant host stand with three blank price cards
image.brief: 식당 입구 예약 데스크 위 태블릿과 빈 가격 카드 세 장. 노트북을 든 창업자가 고민하는 장면. 따뜻한 조명의 레스토랑 배경. 실제 로고나 앱 화면 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should the price grow with?
body: Mira's restaurants get more from the software when more diners book through it. Most share one tablet at the host stand.

options.feedback: Common in software, but here nothing grows. One tablet means one login, so the four-site chain pays almost what the café pays, and staff start sharing passwords.
The bill grows with the value: filled tables. Bands keep it predictable, so owners don't feel taxed on each busy night.
Easy to explain, but the tiny café and the 200-seat bistro pay the same. Set it high and you lose the café; set it low and you undercharge the bistro.

cards.title: Say you chose booking bands. What else separates the plans?
body: Limits alone set the size of each plan. Now decide what makes each one worth picking.

options.text: Same features in every plan; only the booking limits differ
options.feedback: Clear and fair, but a busy bistro losing money to no-shows has no reason to upgrade until it hits the limit.

options.text: Build each plan around a type of restaurant: small café, busy dinner spot, multi-site group
options.feedback: Each owner sees a plan made for them. The bistro pays more for deposits and reminder texts because no-shows hurt it most.

options.text: Every feature in every plan; higher plans get faster support
options.feedback: Support costs you staff time on every upgrade, and most owners rarely need it. You'd give away the features they would pay for.

cards.title: Say you chose plans by restaurant type. Now set the prices.
body: Basic, for small cafés, is $39 a month. What should Plus (busy dinner spots) and Group (several sites) cost?

options.feedback: Gentle steps feel friendly. But single restaurants jump to Group for $20 more, and the chain pays far less than the value it gets from four sites.
Each price matches what that restaurant gains. Group is priced for chains, and next to it Plus looks like a reasonable choice for a busy bistro.
Plus becomes a decoy that makes Group look cheap. It may lift Group sales, but single restaurants who only need deposits feel pushed and may leave.

cards.title: Three plans, three kinds of restaurant
body: Each step up adds what that kind of restaurant values most, not just more of the same.

breakdown.label: Basic
breakdown.detail: Up to 300 bookings a month. Online booking and table plan. For small cafés.

breakdown.label: Plus
breakdown.detail: Up to 1,500 bookings. Adds deposits, reminder texts and a waitlist. For busy dinner spots.

breakdown.label: Group
breakdown.detail: Up to 3 sites, no booking limit. Adds shared guest list and reports across sites.

cards.title: Customers sorted themselves.
body: Mira never asked anyone what they could afford. The café picked Basic. Both bistros picked Plus for the deposits. The pizza chain chose Group, then asked about a fourth site.
That's the quiet power of good plans. Each customer pays close to the value they get, because **they choose the plan that fits them**.
cards.callout: The same three questions work for a restaurant's own catering menu: price per guest, packages for office lunch vs wedding, and steps that match the value.
cards.softwareNote: In software, adding a customer costs little, so plan design, not cost, decides most of the margin.

cards.title: Limits can feel like punishment.
body: Booking bands work until a café has a huge December and gets a surprise upgrade notice. Hard cut-offs on a good month feel like a penalty for success.
Give a grace period or a gentle warning. And treat launch prices as a first guess. After a few months, check which plan people pick and where they get stuck, then adjust.

cards.title: Three plans answer three questions.
list: **Decision 1 → Charging by the unit of value:** price grows with what the customer gains
**Decision 2 → Good, better, best:** each tier built for a different type of customer
**Decision 3 → Price steps and anchoring:** gaps that match value, with the top plan framing the middle
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down what your price grows with, who each option is for, and whether each step up is worth its gap.
